# Contents

# 1 Introduction

`stabl()` is the high-level entry point to **stablr**. Given a table of
features and an outcome, it runs STABL with statistically safe defaults and
returns an object that states, in plain language, which features were selected
and how reliable the selection is estimated to be.

The full contract is as follows.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- stabl(my_data, y = "response")
fit
```

Everything else in the package is available when more control is required;
see Section 4, The expert interface.

# 2 A worked example

The example uses a small simulated proteomic-style dataset: 60 samples and 8
features, of which two truly drive the outcome.

```{r data}
set.seed(1L)
df <- data.frame(
  m1 = rnorm(60), m2 = rnorm(60), m3 = rnorm(60), m4 = rnorm(60),
  m5 = rnorm(60), n1 = rnorm(60), n2 = rnorm(60), n3 = rnorm(60)
)
df$response <- 0.9 * df$m1 + 0.9 * df$m2 + rnorm(60, sd = 0.4)
```

STABL is fitted with a reduced number of bootstraps so that the vignette knits
quickly; the default (`n_bootstraps = 1000`) should be used in practice.

```{r fit, message = FALSE}
library(stablr)
fit <- stabl(df, y = "response", n_bootstraps = 200L, random_state = 1L)
```

Printing the fit gives the plain-language answer.

```{r print}
fit
```

The printed output reports the selected features together with the estimated
reliability of the selection.

The selected features are also available as a character vector.

```{r names}
feature_names(fit)
```

`summary()` adds the stability threshold and the FDP+ estimate.

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The `plot()` method draws the stability paths and the FDP+ curve.

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

The figure shows the stability paths of the features across the lambda grid
together with the FDP+ curve used for calibration.

# 3 Defaults chosen by `stabl()`

| Decision | Default chosen | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Artificial features | model-X knockoffs (`knockoff_equi`) | the pairing validated for FDP+ calibration; the raw `random_permutation` default of the expert interface is anti-conservative for multivariate learners |
| Calibration | FDP+ on (no fixed `hard_threshold`) | the threshold is chosen to control the estimated false discovery proportion rather than fixed by hand |
| Knockoff failure | `knockoff_fallback = "stop"` | a silent fallback would silently change what the FDP+ estimates mean |
| Lambda grid | automatic | a sensible grid is derived from the data |

Any expert argument --- `artificial_proportion`, `sample_fraction`,
`sample_groups`, a custom adapter --- is passed through `...`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- stabl(df, y = "response", base_learner = "elastic_net",
             artificial_proportion = 0.5)
```

# 4 The expert interface

`stabl()` is a thin wrapper around `stabl_fit()`, the expert interface with
full control over all arguments (lambda grids, bootstrap design, thresholds,
learner adapters, grouping). Every `stabl()` result is also a valid
`stabl_fit` object, so the entire expert toolkit applies unchanged.

```{r expert}
# accessors (identical on stabl and stabl_fit objects)
head(get_stabl_scores(fit))
get_fdrs(fit)

# the multiomic workflows, metrics, and plotting helpers all accept
# stabl_fit objects — including the one you just built with stabl()
class(fit)
```

The printed accessors show the stability scores, the FDP+ summary, and the
class of the fitted object, which confirms that a `stabl()` result can be
treated as a `stabl_fit` object. Read `?stabl_fit` for the full expert
interface, and the other vignettes for multi-omic workflows, nested
cross-validation, and environment stability.

# 5 Compatibility with versions before 0.3.0

Nothing is removed. A number of ambiguous names were renamed
(`get_feature_names_out()` is now `get_feature_names()`,
`stacked_multi_omic()` is now `stabl_multiomic_stacked()`,
`jaccard_matrix()` is now `jaccard_similarity_matrix()`, and so on; see
`NEWS.md` for the full table). The old names continue to work: each warns once
and delegates to the new name.
